name: SCALE
description: SCALE measures how engineering best practices are Standardized, Consumed, Automated, Leveraged, and made Effective across an organization. It is the narrative layer over detailed maturity metrics: its purpose is to make hundreds of metrics readable as a small number of aspect-level storylines.

narratives.title: Why SCALE exists
narratives.body: Maturity frameworks make it cheap to generate hundreds of metrics, and cheap metrics destroy the story. Leadership cannot act on "maturity level 3 became level 4" repeated three hundred times. SCALE organizes every metric under one of five aspects — Standards, Consumption, Automation, Leverage, Effectiveness — so the platform story can be told in five sentences, each backed by drill-down evidence. Domain dimensions (ordered lifecycles) provide each discipline's own story spine, orthogonal to the horizontal aspect view.

domains.name: API Best Practices
domains.description: Consistent, machine-validated API design across all services, anchored by api-style-spec: executable style rules, conformance levels, and generated SDKs.

dimensions.name: API Lifecycle
dimensions.description: The journey of an API from design through evolution.

stages.name: Design
stages.description: API design and review against the style guide.

stages.name: Development
stages.description: Implementation with linting and OpenAPI validation.

stages.name: Publication
stages.description: Documentation, SDK generation, and catalog listing.

stages.name: Consumption
stages.description: Client integration and SDK usage.

stages.name: Evolution
stages.description: Versioning, deprecation, and breaking-change management.

capabilities.name: API Style Conformance
capabilities.description: Services design and validate APIs against the organization's api-style-spec profile.

metrics.name: Style guide rule coverage
metrics.description: Percentage of API design categories covered by executable rules in the organization's api-style-spec profile, per the api-coverage rubric.

metrics.name: Services enrolled in API linting
metrics.description: Percentage of API-serving services with api-style-spec linting configured.

metrics.name: APIs passing silver conformance
metrics.description: Percentage of linted APIs that pass the silver conformance level. Adoption says the linter is installed; this says the APIs actually conform.

metrics.name: APIs with blocking CI validation
metrics.description: Percentage of API repositories where style validation blocks merge rather than warning.

metrics.name: Client SDKs generated from OpenAPI
metrics.description: Percentage of client SDKs generated from conformant OpenAPI rather than hand-written.

metrics.name: Unplanned breaking changes per quarter
metrics.description: Count of consumer-reported breaking API changes that were not part of a planned deprecation.

levelCriteria.M1: Style guide documented; manual reviews only.
levelCriteria.M3: CI validation standard across teams; conformance levels tracked.
levelCriteria.M4: Blocking CI enforcement; >=95% of APIs at silver conformance.
levelCriteria.M5: AI-assisted design review and automated remediation with measurably better outcomes.

capabilities.name: OpenAPI Quality
capabilities.description: OpenAPI documents are complete enough to drive documentation, validation, and SDK generation.

metrics.name: OpenAPI completeness score
metrics.description: Mean completeness score of OpenAPI documents (descriptions, examples, schemas) per the style-guide-quality rubric.

narratives.title: Why API standardization matters
narratives.body: Every inconsistent API is a permanent tax: longer reviews, hand-written clients, breaking changes discovered by consumers. An executable style guide (api-style-spec) turns API design from tribal review knowledge into CI-enforced conformance, and conformant OpenAPI unlocks generated SDKs — leverage that compounds with every new service.

domains.name: Observability Best Practices
domains.description: Every service emits standardized telemetry — OpenTelemetry/Prometheus with Golden Signals and RED/USE coverage — and that telemetry is demonstrably good enough to run the business on.

dimensions.name: Telemetry Lifecycle
dimensions.description: The journey of telemetry from instrumentation to optimization.

stages.name: Instrumentation
stages.description: SDKs installed and signals emitted.

stages.name: Collection
stages.description: Pipelines, storage, and semantic-convention conformance.

stages.name: Analysis
stages.description: Dashboards and service-level indicators.

stages.name: Alerting
stages.description: Actionable alerts tied to SLOs.

stages.name: Optimization
stages.description: Cost, cardinality, and signal-quality tuning.

capabilities.name: OpenTelemetry Instrumentation
capabilities.description: Services are instrumented with OpenTelemetry (or Prometheus exporters) and emit the Four Golden Signals.

metrics.name: Telemetry profile coverage
metrics.description: Percentage of service archetypes with a published telemetry profile (required signals, semantic conventions).

metrics.name: Services with OTel SDK
metrics.description: Percentage of production services with the OpenTelemetry SDK (or Prometheus exporter) installed.

metrics.name: Services emitting Golden Signals
metrics.description: Percentage of instrumented services actually emitting latency, traffic, errors, and saturation per the telemetry profile. Installation is adoption; emission is conformance.

metrics.name: Services using auto-instrumentation
metrics.description: Percentage of instrumented services using auto-instrumentation rather than hand-written spans for baseline signals.

metrics.name: Dashboards from shared templates
metrics.description: Percentage of service dashboards generated from shared templates rather than built per-service.

metrics.name: Mean time to restore
metrics.description: Mean time to restore service for production incidents, in minutes.

frameworks.description: Golden Signals per the Google SRE book.
Current practice: distributed tracing and proactive alerting place us at Stage 2 of 4; Stage 3 requires AI/ML anomaly detection and automated remediation.
Foundation in place; value-driver practices are still largely reactive.

levelCriteria.M2: OTel SDK available; some services instrumented.
levelCriteria.M3: Telemetry profile published; majority of services emitting Golden Signals.
levelCriteria.M5: Auto-instrumentation by default with predictive signal-quality analysis.

capabilities.name: RED/USE Methodology
capabilities.description: Request-serving services expose RED metrics (rate, errors, duration); infrastructure exposes USE metrics (utilization, saturation, errors).

metrics.name: Request-serving services with RED metrics
metrics.description: Percentage of request-serving services exposing rate, errors, and duration metrics per the profile.

metrics.name: Incidents detected by alerts
metrics.description: Percentage of production incidents detected by alerting before a customer or engineer report — the test of whether the telemetry is actually good.

frameworks.description: RED/USE dashboards and alerting correspond to Stage 2 practice.
Alert-first incident detection is proactive-level practice for the uptime value driver.

narratives.title: Why observability standardization matters
narratives.body: Installing a telemetry SDK is not observability. The journey is adoption (SDK installed), conformance (Golden Signals and RED/USE actually emitted with correct semantic conventions), and effectiveness (the signals are good enough that incidents are detected by alerts, not by customers). Standardized telemetry also creates leverage: shared dashboards and alert templates that every service inherits instead of rebuilding.

domains.name: Platform Adoption
domains.description: Adoption and leverage of internal platform libraries across the organization's Go repositories. Measures how shared infrastructure (agent frameworks, utilities, tooling) is standardized, consumed, and creates leverage.

dimensions.name: Platform Library Lifecycle
dimensions.description: The journey of a platform library from inception to widespread leverage.

stages.name: Foundation
stages.description: Library exists with clear API, documentation, and versioning.

stages.name: Adoption
stages.description: Teams discover and integrate the library into their services.

stages.name: Conformance
stages.description: Adopters use the library correctly per documented patterns.

stages.name: Leverage
stages.description: Shared improvements benefit all adopters; patterns compound.

stages.name: Evolution
stages.description: Breaking changes are managed; deprecations are smooth.

capabilities.name: Core Utilities Adoption
capabilities.description: Adoption of foundational utility libraries (mogo, gohttp, etc.) that provide common patterns for error handling, HTTP clients, configuration, and data structures.

metrics.name: Core utilities library exists
metrics.description: The mogo library provides documented, tested utilities for common Go patterns.

target.description: Library exists with godoc, tests, and semver

metrics.name: Repos importing mogo
metrics.description: Percentage of organization Go repositories that directly depend on github.com/grokify/mogo.

metrics.name: Repos importing gohttp
metrics.description: Percentage of organization Go repositories that directly depend on github.com/grokify/gohttp.

capabilities.name: AI Agent Framework Adoption
capabilities.description: Adoption of the omniagent framework for building AI-powered agents with consistent patterns for tool handling, context management, and model integration.

metrics.name: Agent framework exists
metrics.description: The omniagent library provides a documented, tested framework for building AI agents.

target.description: Framework exists with godoc, tests, and examples

metrics.name: Repos importing omniagent
metrics.description: Count of organization Go repositories that directly depend on github.com/plexusone/omniagent.

metrics.name: Shared tools across agents
metrics.description: Number of tool implementations in omniagent/tools that are reused by multiple agent projects.

capabilities.name: Initiative Tracking Adoption
capabilities.description: Adoption of VisionStudio for tracking initiatives, roadmaps, and engineering metrics across projects.

metrics.name: Initiative tracking system exists
metrics.description: VisionStudio provides initiative, phase, and RMI tracking with dashboard visualization.

metrics.name: Repositories tracked in VisionStudio
metrics.description: Number of repositories registered and actively tracked in VisionStudio.

metrics.name: Initiatives with ROADMAP.md
metrics.description: Percentage of tracked initiatives that have a structured ROADMAP.md with RMIs.

capabilities.name: Git Tooling Adoption
capabilities.description: Adoption of gogit for repository scanning, dependency analysis, and commit statistics.

metrics.name: Git tooling library exists
metrics.description: The gogit library provides repository discovery, commit parsing, and dependency analysis.

metrics.name: Repos importing gogit
metrics.description: Count of organization Go repositories that directly depend on github.com/grokify/gogit.

metrics.name: Repos with gitscan in CI
metrics.description: Count of repositories using gitscan for pre-push validation or dependency ordering.

capabilities.name: SCALE Metrics Adoption
capabilities.description: Adoption of the SCALE framework for measuring and narrating platform maturity.

metrics.name: SCALE framework exists
metrics.description: The SCALE library provides framework, domain, and assessment modeling with rollup computation.

metrics.name: SCALE domains defined
metrics.description: Number of SCALE domains with active capabilities and metrics.

metrics.name: SCALE assessments per quarter
metrics.description: Number of SCALE assessments produced per quarter with journey narratives.

capabilities.name: Dependency Health
capabilities.description: Cross-cutting metrics on dependency hygiene across the organization's Go repositories.

metrics.name: Repos without replace directives
metrics.description: Percentage of Go repositories with no local replace directives in go.mod.

metrics.name: Repos with matching module names
metrics.description: Percentage of Go repositories where go.mod module name matches the directory structure.

metrics.name: Release order automated
metrics.description: Whether gitscan order is used to determine correct release order for interdependent modules.

metrics.name: Dependency conflicts per quarter
metrics.description: Count of incidents caused by version conflicts or incompatible transitive dependencies.

capabilities.name: Platform Leverage
capabilities.description: Cross-cutting metrics measuring the compound value created by platform adoption.

metrics.name: Internal dependency ratio
metrics.description: Average ratio of internal (organization) dependencies to external dependencies per repository.

target.description: 30% of deps are internal platform libs

metrics.name: Lines of code reused via platform libs
metrics.description: Estimated lines of code not written because platform libraries provide the functionality.

metrics.name: Bugs fixed once, benefit all
metrics.description: Count of bugs fixed in platform libraries that automatically benefited all adopters via version bump.

narratives.title: Why platform adoption matters
narratives.body: Every team building infrastructure from scratch is duplicating effort and diverging from proven patterns. Platform libraries encode best practices once and let every adopter benefit from fixes, optimizations, and new capabilities. Measuring adoption via dependency analysis makes the platform story concrete: we know exactly which repos consume which libraries, and can track adoption growth over time. High adoption with low conformance signals integration problems; low adoption signals discovery or onboarding gaps.

domains.name: Security Best Practices
domains.description: AI-era application security platformized across the delivery lifecycle: from AI threat modeling at design time to an AI-augmented SOC in operations.

dimensions.name: Security Lifecycle
dimensions.description: AI-native security across the software delivery lifecycle.

stages.name: Design & Planning
stages.description: AI Threat Modeling: architecture reviews, security requirements, and risk analysis at design time.

narratives.body: Threat modeling has historically been rationed — a scarce expert activity reserved for critical systems. AI collapses its cost, so every service can have a current threat model. The measure of this stage is coverage: threat modeling as a default, not an exception.

stages.name: Development
stages.description: Defensive Hygiene: secure coding, dependency management, and secrets management during implementation.

stages.name: CI/CD Pipeline
stages.description: Automated Posture: SAST, SCA, secrets detection, SBOM generation, and policy enforcement in the pipeline.

stages.name: Offensive Validation
stages.description: AI Pentesting & Red Teams: adversary simulation and validation exercises, augmented and scaled by AI.

stages.name: Operations
stages.description: AI SOC / CSIRT / PSIRT: AI-augmented detection, incident response, and product security response.

capabilities.name: AI Threat Modeling
capabilities.description: Services carry current, AI-assisted threat models reviewed at design time.

metrics.name: Services with current threat models
metrics.description: Percentage of production services with a threat model updated within the last two quarters.

capabilities.name: Automated Pipeline Posture
capabilities.description: Security scanning (SAST, SCA, secrets) runs and blocks in every delivery pipeline.

metrics.name: Pipelines with blocking security gates
metrics.description: Percentage of delivery pipelines where SAST, SCA, and secrets detection run as blocking gates.

frameworks.description: OWASP ASVS verification via pipeline automation.

capabilities.name: AI Security Operations
capabilities.description: AI-augmented SOC, CSIRT, and PSIRT: triage, enrichment, and response assisted by AI agents.

metrics.name: Security incident mean time to restore
metrics.description: Mean time to contain and restore for security incidents, in hours.

narratives.title: The AI-era security story
narratives.body: Compliance frameworks like NIST CSF tell the auditor's story. This dimension tells the transformation story: security is shifting from human gatekeeping at a few chokepoints to AI-native practice at every lifecycle stage — AI threat modeling in design, defensive hygiene in development, automated posture in the pipeline, AI pentesting and red teams for offensive validation, and an AI-augmented SOC/CSIRT/PSIRT in operations. The maturity of each stage, read left to right, is the journey.

externalModels.name: AWS Observability Maturity Model
externalModels.description: AWS's four-stage observability maturity model from the AWS Observability Best Practices guide. Levels are the source's own; the PRISM crosswalk is an explicit SCALE mapping, not part of the AWS model.

levels.name: Foundational monitoring
levels.description: Basic monitoring exists in inconsistent forms across teams; no defined strategy for a complete view of applications across the organization.

levels.name: Intermediate monitoring
levels.description: More sophisticated practices adopted: proactive alerting and distributed tracing provide insight into interactions between systems.

levels.name: Advanced observability
levels.description: Automated remediation plus AI/ML-driven anomaly detection and root-cause analysis enable corrective action before end-user impact.

levels.name: Proactive observability
levels.description: Proactive and predictive observability practices with advanced automation.

externalModels.name: New Relic Observability Maturity
externalModels.description: New Relic's observability maturity series organizes practice by value drivers (intelligent observability as the Level 0 foundation, then business uptime, digital experience, engineering excellence), each progressing reactive → proactive → mastery. This codification normalizes that structure onto a single ladder; the source organizes by value driver, and the PRISM crosswalk is an explicit SCALE mapping, not part of the New Relic model. Note: New Relic documentation content is published under CC BY-NC-SA — this file intentionally carries only level structure and short paraphrases with attribution.

levels.name: Level 0 — Intelligent observability foundation
levels.description: The essential foundation (instrumentation and platform capability) that enables all other observability value drivers.

levels.name: Reactive
levels.description: Value-driver practices applied reactively — responding to problems after they surface.

levels.name: Proactive
levels.description: Practices applied proactively — anticipating and preventing problems.

levels.name: Mastery
levels.description: Mature, continuously improving practice tied to measurable business value.
